item.title: Randomization to Balance Performance under Nominal and Compromised Communication
item.description: arXiv:2610.31957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is well-known that under nominal communication, where agents are able to share information with one another, game-theoretic methods provide system-level performance guarantees in multiagent cyber-physical human systems such as distributed resource allocation. However, approaches that depend on communication are frequently not robust when communication is compromised. While randomized decision-making can prevent arbitrarily poor outcomes under compromised communication, these performance guarantees often do not improve when communication abilities are restored. Thus, it remains unclear whether a single approach can perform well under nominal communication and remain robust under compromised communication. In this paper, we study whether a system operator can inform agents about how much they should randomize their choice when selecting actions in order to balance performance across both settings. We show that for any scenario (e.g., a multiagent resource allocation instance), there exists a level of randomization where nominal efficiency is near-optimal while compromised efficiency is strictly positive. We then show that this guarantee weakens as agents must choose between increasingly many resources. These results provide an initial step toward understanding randomization as a tool for robust performance across communication settings.
item.dc:creator: Colton Hill, Brandon Collins, Philip N. Brown

item.title: Differentiable Combinatorial Auction Design: Optimizing Revenue-Welfare-Fairness Frontiers With Graph Attention Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.31977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing optimal auctions for allocating public infrastructure-such as airport slots and energy resources-is challenging due to interdependent resources and complex side-constraints. While the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction guarantees maximum welfare, it cannot maximize revenue or accommodate the multi-objective trade-offs inherent in public infrastructure systems. We propose a differentiable, constraint-aware framework for combinatorial auction design that enables end-to-end learning of fractionally feasible, approximately strategy-proof mechanisms. Our primary contribution is a combinatorial constraint enforcement technique that ensures fractional feasibility by construction, bypassing the need for penalty-based approximations. We introduce CAGraph, a novel graph-based architecture designed to capture dependencies between items and bidders, alongside CANet and CAFormer as deep learning baselines, for combinatorial settings. We also provide a Matching Pursuit-inspired decomposition that maps fractional allocations to feasible discrete allocations and empirically evaluates the resulting discretization gap. In synthetic benchmarks and an airport slot-divestiture case study, respectively, the learned mechanisms achieve up to 73.5% and 180% higher expected revenue than VCG, under small empirical regret. Finally, we visualize the Pareto frontiers for revenue, welfare, and fairness, providing regulators with a decision-support tool to design infrastructure auctions that balance profitability, efficiency and equity.
item.dc:creator: Mai Pham, Vikrant Vaze, Peter Chin

item.title: Capacity Modification for Matching with Couples: An Integer Programming and Computational Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.32793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study capacity modification in the Hospitals/Residents problem with Couples, in which hospital capacities and a stable matching are jointly determined. Exact and Cutoff integer programming formulations are developed for the resulting problem. We assume that, for each couple, either both members are matched or neither is. For arbitrary strict preferences, every instance admits a stable matching after changing each hospital capacity by at most two. Total capacity increases by at most one, and this bound is tight. Under sub-responsive and sub-complete couple preferences, a stable matching exists after adding at most one position to each hospital. The total number of additions is at most the number of couples, and this bound is also tight. Computational experiments show that Exact formulations are modestly faster at fixed capacities, whereas Cutoff formulations perform substantially better in the minimum repair experiments and attain higher completion rates in markets with up to 30,000 doctors. Across 96,000 synthetic and reconstructed markets, small capacity changes restore existence whenever no stable matching exists at the original capacities.
item.dc:creator: Zexiao Wu, Genjiu Xu, P\'eter Bir\'o

item.title: Pareto-optimal Scheduling with Predictions
item.description: arXiv:2610.32503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study preemptive single-machine scheduling with predictions, where a prediction of the order of the jobs (or of their sizes) is available, and the objective is to minimize the total completion time. An algorithm is $c$-consistent if it is $c$-competitive when the prediction is correct, and $R$-robust if it is $R$-competitive whatever the prediction. Since the introduction of this problem as one of the first examples of learning-augmented algorithms, the best possible trade-off between consistency and robustness has remained open. We determine it exactly for deterministic algorithms. For every $R>2$, we give an $R$-robust algorithm whose consistency is \[ c(R)=R\Big(1-\Big(1-\frac{R+2}{R^2}\Big)^{\frac R{R+2}}\Big), \] and we prove that no deterministic $R$-robust algorithm, with either predicted order or predicted job sizes, has better consistency. In particular, consistency $1+\eps$ is achievable with robustness $\eps^{-1/2}+\frac16+O(\sqrt\eps)$, whereas all previous algorithms required robustness $\Theta(1/\eps)$. Our algorithm is greedy: it follows the predicted order as fast as possible, subject to the invariant that the cost paid so far is at most $R$ times the optimum of the instance in which every unfinished job would end immediately. The matching lower bound rests on the observation that every robust deterministic algorithm must satisfy the same invariant along its run on correct predictions.
item.dc:creator: Ziyad Benomar, Vianney Perchet

item.title: Social Welfare in Budget Aggregation
item.description: arXiv:2602.23027v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study budget aggregation under $\ell_1$-utilities, a model in which agents with heterogeneous preferences allocate a public budget across alternatives. Each agent reports their preferred allocation, and a mechanism selects an allocation. Early work has focused on social welfare maximization, which admits truthful mechanisms but may underrepresent minority groups, motivating the study of proportional mechanisms. However, the dominant proportionality notion, single-minded proportionality, is weak, as it only constrains outcomes when agents hold extreme preferences. To understand proportionality and its interaction with welfare and truthfulness, we address three questions. First, how much welfare must be sacrificed to achieve proportionality? We formalize this via the price of proportionality, the best worst-case welfare ratio between a proportional mechanism and the welfare-maximizing allocation. We introduce a single-minded proportional and truthful mechanism, UtilProp, and show it achieves the optimal worst-case ratio. Second, how do proportional mechanisms compare in welfare? We define an instance-wise welfare dominance relation and compare existing mechanisms, finding that UtilProp welfare-dominates all previously known single-minded proportional and truthful mechanisms. Third, can stronger proportionality notions be achieved without compromising welfare guarantees? We answer affirmatively by studying decomposability and proposing GreedyDecomp, a decomposable mechanism with optimal worst-case welfare ratio.
item.dc:creator: Javier Cembrano, Rupert Freeman, Ulrike Schmidt-Kraepelin, Markus Utke

item.title: STAKE: Preventing a colluding majority from double spending
item.description: arXiv:2610.01169v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Blockchains typically operate in open networks where it is hard to control the delay of messages. While classic blockchain protocols assumed synchrony, newer protocols try to remain secure despite unexpected network delays. Unfortunately, in the traditional model where $n$ participants can either be honest or Byzantine, we need a supermajority, or $\lfloor 2n/3\rfloor + 1$, of them to be honest. Recent work have explored the question of reducing the number of needed honest nodes in a game theory model to a majority sometimes by introducing $k$ rational players and $t$ Byzantine players. Yet, to our knowledge, no blockchain protocol managed to reduce it further. In this paper, we offer a blockchain protocol called Secure and Tolerant Algorithm through ($k,t$)-robust Equilibrium (STAKE) that works with only $\lfloor n/3\rfloor + 1$ honest players. STAKE requires each consensus participant to stake a sufficiently large amount $s$ compared to their liquidity $\ell$. We show that the probability that a coalition manages to execute $\zeta$ double spending attacks (we call them a $\zeta$-uple attack) drops exponentially fast with $\zeta$. This allows us to demonstrate that STAKE reaches a ($k,t$)-robust equilibrium, or that rational players do not collude with Byzantine, even with a relatively low $s/\ell$ ratio.
item.dc:creator: Zahra Naderi, Vincent Gramoli

item.title: Temporal Fair Division in Multi-Agent Systems: From Precise Alternation Metrics to Scalable Coordination Proxies
item.description: arXiv:2605.14879v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many multi-agent games and simulated environments involve several independent, often learning, agents repeatedly competing for a shared resource. Conventional fairness measures assess whether resources are shared equally overall, but cannot distinguish orderly turn-taking from irregular access patterns that produce long, unpredictable waiting times despite similar cumulative outcomes. We introduce Rotational Periodicity, a family of computationally efficient metrics combining two complementary measurements, the regularity of waiting times between successful accesses and the balance of access frequencies across agents. We evaluate them against a more detailed family of alternation metrics in a repeated threshold-congestion game, the Honey-Jar Game, in which two to ten reinforcement-learning agents compete for exclusive access to a shared high-value resource. Our experiments show that independently trained Q-learning agents often coordinate substantially worse than random-policy agents, even though conventional fairness metrics consistently report favourable outcomes. Every member of the family closely reproduces the rankings of the more computationally expensive alternation metrics, while computing six to twenty times faster as the number of agents grows. A direct timing study, which separates the two quantities that drive that cost, measures the advantage growing in proportion to the number of agents out to two thousand agents. item.title: The fixed-point bundle method over product-of-simplex domains arising from game equilibria
item.description: arXiv:2609.16158v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Developing general-purpose algorithms with global asymptotic convergence guarantees for Nash equilibria of general-sum games remains a longstanding challenge. This paper extends the fixed-point bundle framework for finite-dimensional variational inequalities (VIs) from simplex domains to product-of-simplex domains, enabling its direct application to Nash equilibrium computation. The resulting fixed-point bundle exhibits a composite fiber bundle structure. The key innovation is to construct an equivalent VI on a simplex and establish the equivalence between the two fixed-point bundle frameworks via a fiber bundle isomorphism. Exploiting this geometric equivalence, we show that the path-following algorithm for VIs on product-of-simplex domains inherits the global linear convergence guarantees of the simplex-domain framework. In numerical experiments, the algorithm attained a precision of $10^{-5}$ on all 5600 randomly generated game instances, with dimension ranging from 2-player 128-action to 128-player 2-action. Code and data are available at https://github.com/shb20tsinghua/FiberBundle_VI.
item.dc:creator: Hongbo Sun

item.title: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.16770v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Next-generation wireless networks are expected to support high data rates and reliable connectivity while meeting requirements for energy efficiency, resource management, and communication security. Digital Twin (DT) technology represents expected network behavior and enables the actual network state to be assessed against it. Integrating DT technology with reinforcement learning (RL) supports adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making. This paper presents a simulation-based DT reference and a belief-guided Q-learning (BGQL) method for joint jammer identification and beam-power control in a site-specific 28-GHz network model. Receiver-level residuals between attack-free and attacked configurations are combined with candidate spatial jamming footprints and accumulated into a normalized suspicion vector. BGQL incorporates this vector into its state, reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. Compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs per configuration, with known jammer counts, BGQL achieves link-rate scores of 437.4-564.2 Mbit/s, rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37-76.79 Mbit/J, and localization recall of 100% for one jammer and 78%-81% for two jammers. BGQL requires 80-130 s per run versus 5-14 s for SARSA. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided learning for security-aware beam-power control in 6G networks.
item.dc:creator: Parmida Geranmayeh, Onur G\"unl\"u
